name: Callipogon proletarius
intro: Females lay their eggs in the cracks of white-rotted hardwood logs. I collect the eggs while they are still in those cracks and rear the hatchlings individually. The young larvae are highly cannibalistic.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: The nominate form is recorded from Puerto Rico

facts.title: When to separate the brood
facts.text: Collect eggs before hatching and house each one separately

facts.title: Unsuccessful larval substrate
facts.text: All larvae in the oyster-kinshi group died

facts.title: Adult size record
facts.text: 75 mm body length for the type specimen in Berlin (Prioninae of the World)

sections.title: Laying logs and egg collection
sections.text: I give the female a white-rotted hardwood log with accessible cracks. The cracks themselves are the places to inspect for eggs. I check the laying log while the female is using it and remove eggs individually as I find them. Each egg gets its own rearing space so that the hatchlings never share a piece of wood. Waiting until larvae are visible risks losing siblings to cannibalism.

sections.title: Hatching and time in culture
sections.text: In the Puerto Rican culture, an adult was photographed in January 2026 and hatchlings were present on January 30. The earliest eggs have no recorded laying date, so their incubation time is unknown. Larvae on turkey-tail kinshi were still growing in early November, roughly nine months after the January hatch. The brood record ends at the feeding stage and gives no date for pupation or adult emergence.

sections.title: Larvae
sections.text: I reared larvae on two kinds of kinshi (fungus-colonized wood). By early November the larvae on turkey-tail kinshi were growing well. All those on oyster-mushroom kinshi had died, although most of my Stenodontes exsertus larvae on the same batch survived. I would start another group on turkey-tail kinshi. I followed this brood through the feeding stage.

sections.title: Adult size in the Puerto Rican species
sections.text: Prioninae of the World lists the Berlin type specimen of Callipogon proletarius at 75 mm in body length. That measurement belongs to one museum specimen. The January adult in this breeding account was photographed without a recorded body measurement.

sections.title: How the Korean team reared the relict longhorn
sections.text:
Lee et al. (2021, pp. 4–6, fig. 3) obtained 16 eggs from a 78 mm female Callipogon relictus found on July 20, 2017, in Gwangneung Forest, South Korea. Each larva grew in its own container. The first two instars occupied Petri dishes. The team then used 850 mL bottles for intermediate instars and 4.2 L bottles for large larvae. At the prepupal stage they moved individuals into plastic containers for the final molt. The authors report 20 ± 5 °C and 35 ± 1% humidity for the rearing environment.
Lee and colleagues also watched three infertile females examine oak and hornbeam bark with their antennae and probe fissures with their ovipositors. Inspection of the cracks yielded no eggs (fig. 8A). The eggs found in white-rotted log cracks in our Puerto Rican culture provide a separate, direct laying record for Callipogon proletarius.

sections.title: Published development times and size records
sections.text:
Lee et al. (2021, pp. 10–12, figs. 5–7) give individual body lengths for wild Korean adults. A male found on August 14, 2017 measured 60 mm. On August 6, 2018 the team found a 98 mm male, followed on August 14 by an 88 mm female. In their review, the authors cite earlier estimates of five to seven years inside the host tree.
Kuprin et al. (2014, pp. 1251–1255) followed Callipogon relictus from egg to adult under controlled conditions. They packed 2–3 L containers with Japanese elm sawdust and kept them at 25 °C and 65–75% humidity. Twice a month they recorded larval mass, body length and head-capsule width. Females placed single eggs in bark cracks. Eggs took about 20 days to hatch, the larval stage lasted about 42 months and pupae took 21–25 days. Total development took about 44 months. Most adults lived 14–28 days.
In that study, head-capsule width increased from 1.1–2.3 mm in the first instar (82 larvae measured) to 8.2–8.7 mm in the sixth (24 measured). The authors also observed older larvae eating younger larvae. These measurements and stage durations apply to the relict longhorn. For the Puerto Rican species, the dates from our own brood are given above.

sections.title: A fungal diet trial in the relict longhorn
sections.text:
Yi, Kuprin, Lee and Bae (2017) started 53 Callipogon relictus larvae on mycelium of the white-rot fungus Pleurotus florida on August 11, 2015. They reared the larvae at 25 °C and 60% relative humidity in constant darkness, without a diapause period. From September 10 to October 1, 2016, 11 adults emerged (four males and seven females), about 13 months after the larval trial began. This was 20.8% of the starting group by those dates. Three males exceeded 100 mm, and the largest measured 106.8 mm.
That result is especially relevant to the choice of kinshi. The published trial produced adult relict longhorns on this oyster fungus. In our Puerto Rican brood the oyster-kinshi group died, while larvae on turkey-tail kinshi continued feeding. The two accounts differ in both beetle species and rearing material.
